units.title: Evolutionary Biology
topics: Origin of life: the Oparin–Haldane theory and the Miller–Urey experiment
Evidences of evolution: morphological, anatomical, palaeontological, embryological and biochemical
Lamarckism, Darwinism and Neo-Darwinism
Human evolution from Ramapithecus to modern man

sections.title: Origin of life: the Oparin–Haldane theory and the Miller–Urey experiment
Evidences of evolution: morphological, anatomical, palaeontological, embryological and biochemical
Lamarckism, Darwinism and Neo-Darwinism
Human evolution from Ramapithecus to modern man

summary: Life arose by chemical evolution (Oparin 1924, Haldane 1929) in a reducing atmosphere of CH₄, NH₃, H₂ and water vapour with no free O₂, energised by UV and lightning: monomers → polymers → coacervates/microspheres → protocell → anaerobic heterotroph.
Miller–Urey (1953) sparked CH₄, NH₃, H₂ (2 : 2 : 1) and steam for a week and obtained amino acids (glycine, alanine) — monomers, not life.
Homologous organs (same origin, different use) show divergent evolution; analogous organs (different origin, same use) show convergent evolution; vestigial organs and atavism point to ancestors.
Connecting links — Peripatus, Neopilina, Balanoglossus, lungfish, Archaeopteryx, platypus — and the horse series (Eohippus → Equus, toes 4 → 1) are the classic fossil and living evidence.
Haeckel's biogenetic law (embryos), Nuttall's precipitin test, cytochrome c and the universal genetic code (biochemistry) complete the evidence.
Lamarck (1809): use and disuse + inheritance of acquired characters — refuted by Weismann (22 generations of tailed mice; germplasm theory).
Darwin (1859): overproduction, struggle, variation, natural selection ("survival of the fittest", Spencer); weakness — no theory of variation or heredity. De Vries: mutation, Oenothera.
Neo-Darwinism: mutation + recombination + selection + isolation (+ drift, gene flow); the population evolves; Hardy–Weinberg p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1; Biston betularia is directional selection.

units.title: Animal Diversity and Classification
topics: Diagnostic features and classification of animals from Protozoa to Chordata

sections.title: Diagnostic features and classification of animals from Protozoa to Chordata

summary: Animals are classified by level of organisation, symmetry, germ layers, coelom and segmentation: cellular → Porifera; tissue, radial, diploblastic → Coelenterata; acoelomate → Platyhelminthes; pseudocoelomate → Aschelminthes; schizocoelous protostomes → Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca; enterocoelous deuterostomes → Echinodermata, Hemichord
Protozoa are grouped by locomotion: pseudopodia (Amoeba, Entamoeba), flagella (Euglena, Trypanosoma, Leishmania), none (Sporozoa: Plasmodium), cilia (Paramecium, Balantidium).
Porifera: ostia, osculum, canal system, choanocytes, spicules or spongin, gemmules; Calcarea, Hexactinellida (Euplectella), Demospongiae (Euspongia, Spongilla).
Coelenterata: radial, diploblastic, coelenteron, nematocysts, polyp and medusa, metagenesis in Obelia; Hydrozoa, Scyphozoa, Anthozoa.
Platyhelminthes (flame cells; Fasciola, Taenia) and Aschelminthes (pseudocoel, complete gut, separate sexes; Ascaris, Wuchereria, Ancylostoma, Enterobius).
Annelida: metameres, setae/parapodia, closed circulation, nephridia; Polychaeta (Nereis), Oligochaeta (Pheretima), Hirudinea (Hirudinaria).

Arthropoda, the largest phylum: jointed legs, chitin, haemocoel, open circulation; Crustacea (2 pairs of antennae, gills, green glands), Myriapoda, Insecta (3 pairs of legs, tracheae, Malpighian tubules), Arachnida (4 pairs of legs, book lungs, no antennae).
Mollusca: mantle, shell, radula, ctenidia; seven classes from Neopilina to Sepia; Echinodermata: pentaradial adults, water vascular system, tube feet; Asteroidea to Crinoidea.

units.title: Animal Tissues and Histology
topics: Epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous tissues: structure, location and function

sections.title: Epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous tissues: structure, location and function

summary: A tissue is a group of similar cells with a common origin and function; the four primary tissues are epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous.

Epithelium rests on a basement membrane, has almost no matrix, is avascular and arises from all three germ layers; it is named by layers and cell shape — squamous (alveoli, capillaries), cuboidal (kidney tubules, thyroid), columnar (stomach, intestine), ciliated (oviduct), pseudostratified (trachea), stratified squamous (skin, oesophagus)
Glands are exocrine, endocrine or heterocrine (pancreas), and secrete in merocrine (salivary), apocrine (mammary) or holocrine (sebaceous) fashion.

Connective tissue has few cells (fibroblasts, macrophages, mast cells, plasma cells, fat cells) in abundant matrix with collagen, elastic and reticular fibres: areolar, adipose, tendon, ligament, cartilage, bone, blood and lymph.

Cartilage is avascular with chondrin matrix — hyaline (joints, trachea), elastic (pinna, epiglottis), fibrocartilage (intervertebral discs); bone has ossein and hydroxyapatite, osteocytes in lacunae and Haversian systems.
Blood: 55 % plasma; RBCs (5 million/mm³, 120 days, no nucleus), WBCs (6000–8000/mm³; neutrophils most, basophils fewest, monocytes largest) and platelets (clotting).

Muscle: skeletal (striated, voluntary, multinucleate), smooth (spindle, involuntary) and cardiac (branched, intercalated discs, myogenic); in contraction actin slides over myosin, the A band stays constant and the I band and H zone shorten.

Nervous tissue: neurons (cyton with Nissl granules, dendrites, axon, myelin from Schwann cells or oligodendrocytes, nodes of Ranvier) and neuroglia (astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, Schwann cells, microglia, ependymal cells).

units.title: Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog
topics: Plasmodium: habitat, structure, life cycle and types of malaria
Earthworm (Pheretima): morphology, body systems, physiology and economic importance

sections.title: Plasmodium: habitat, structure, life cycle and types of malaria
Earthworm (Pheretima): morphology, body systems, physiology and economic importance
Frog (Rana): morphology, body systems and physiology

summary: Plasmodium (Sporozoa) is a digenetic intracellular parasite: asexual schizogony in man (intermediate host) — liver cells, then the 48-hour Golgi cycle in RBCs — and sexual phase in the female Anopheles (definitive host) — gametes, zygote, ookinete, oocyst, sporozoites in the salivary glands.
The sporozoite infects man and the gametocyte infects the mosquito; the zygote is the only diploid stage; the fever follows the synchronous bursting of RBCs and the release of haemozoin.
P. vivax (benign tertian, relapses from hypnozoites, commonest in Nepal), P. falciparum (malignant tertian, cerebral malaria), P. malariae (quartan, 72 h) and P. ovale (ovale tertian).
Pheretima posthuma: about 100–120 segments; prostomium; clitellum 14–16; perichaetine setae; female pore 14, male pores 18, papillae 17 and 19, spermathecal pores 5/6–8/9.

Earthworm gut: pharynx 4, gizzard 8–9, stomach 9–14 with calciferous glands, caeca and typhlosole from 26; closed circulation with Hb in plasma and four pairs of hearts (7, 9, 12, 13); cutaneous respiration; septal, integumentary and pharyngeal nephridia.

The earthworm is a protandrous hermaphrodite: testes 10–11, ovaries 13, spermathecae 6–9; cross-fertilisation, fertilisation in the cocoon, direct development; it is the farmer's friend and the basis of vermicomposting.

The frog (Rana tigrina) breathes by skin, buccopharynx and lungs (buccal force pump); its three-chambered heart with sinus venosus and spiral valve gives a double but incomplete circulation; RBCs are nucleated.

The frog is ureotelic with mesonephric kidneys; the male's ureter is a urinogenital duct; it has 10 pairs of cranial nerves, 9 vertebrae and a urostyle; fertilisation is external after amplexus, and thyroxine drives metamorphosis of the tadpole.

units.title: Digestive System
topics: The alimentary canal and the digestive glands
Physiology of digestion and absorption

sections.title: The alimentary canal and the digestive glands
Physiology of digestion and absorption

summary: The canal is a 8–9 m tube of four coats (mucosa, submucosa, muscularis, serosa); the enteric plexus runs peristalsis, modified by vagus (up) and sympathetic (down).

The mouth has 32 permanent teeth, the bolus is made there, and salivary amylase (pH 6.8) starts starch digestion; the three gland pairs are parotid (Stensen's), submandibular (Wharton's) and sublingual (Rivinus).

The stomach secretes 2–3 L of juice at pH 1.5–2.5: parietal cells give HCl and intrinsic factor, chief cells pepsinogen, rennin and lipase, G cells gastrin. HCl activates pepsinogen, kills bacteria and denatures protein; pepsin works only at pH 1.5–2 and stops at peptones.
The small intestine (duodenum 25 cm, jejunum 2.5 m, ileum 3.5 m) receives bile and pancreatic juice, and its folds, villi and microvilli raise the absorptive area to about 200 m².
The liver (1.5 kg, largest gland) makes 0.5–1 L of bile a day at pH 7.6–8.6 with no enzymes; bile salts emulsify fat. The gall bladder stores and concentrates bile and contracts under CCK.

Pancreatic juice (1–1.5 L, pH 8.0–8.3) supplies amylase, trypsin, chymotrypsin, carboxypeptidase, lipase, nucleases and bicarbonate. Enterokinase converts trypsinogen to trypsin, which activates the other two zymogens.
Hormones: gastrin (food → acid), secretin (acid → bicarbonate), CCK (fat → bile + enzymes).

Absorption: monosaccharides and amino acids into blood capillaries → hepatic portal vein → liver; fats as chylomicrons into lacteals → thoracic duct; B₁₂ in the ileum with intrinsic factor; water and salts in the colon.

sections.title: Respiratory organs and the mechanism of breathing
Exchange and transport of gases; regulation of respiration
Respiratory disorders

summary: Air passes nostrils → nasal cavity → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli; the conducting part is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium, the alveolus by simple squamous.
The trachea has 16–20 C-shaped hyaline rings and divides at the carina; the right bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical, so it takes inhaled objects.
The right lung has three lobes, the left two; the pleura holds the lung against the chest wall with a negative intrapleural pressure.
Alveoli number 300–500 million, give 70–80 m² of surface and a 0.5 μm barrier; type II cells make surfactant, without which premature babies get RDS.
Inspiration is active (diaphragm, phrenic C3–C5, plus external intercostals); quiet expiration is passive.
Volumes: TV 500, IRV 3000, ERV 1100, RV 1200 mL; VC = TV + IRV + ERV = 4600; TLC = VC + RV = 5800; FRC = ERV + RV.
Gas exchange is by simple diffusion down partial-pressure gradients: alveolar pO₂ 104, venous 40; venous pCO₂ 45, alveolar 40; CO₂ diffuses about 20× faster than O₂.
O₂: 97 % on haemoglobin, 3 % dissolved; the sigmoid curve has P₅₀ ≈ 27 mmHg and shifts right with CO₂, H⁺, heat and 2,3-BPG (Bohr effect).

sections.title: The heart, the heartbeat, the cardiac cycle and cardiac output
Arterial and venous systems; blood pressure
Blood and blood groups
Cardiovascular disorders

summary: The heart (250–300 g) lies in the mediastinum inside the pericardium; its wall is epicardium, myocardium (thickest in the left ventricle) and endocardium.
Four chambers and four valves: tricuspid and bicuspid (mitral) AV valves with chordae tendineae, and the pulmonary and aortic semilunar valves; all open and close passively.
Double circulation: right ventricle → lungs → left atrium (pulmonary); left ventricle → body → right atrium (systemic). The coronary arteries arise from the ascending aorta.
The SA node (70–80 min⁻¹) is the pacemaker because it depolarises fastest; the impulse passes SA → AV → bundle of His → Purkinje, with a 0.1 s delay at the AV node.
The cardiac cycle lasts 0.8 s: atrial systole 0.1 s, ventricular systole 0.3 s, diastole 0.5 s; S1 is AV valve closure, S2 semilunar closure.
CO = SV × HR ≈ 70 × 72 ≈ 5 L min⁻¹; ejection fraction ≈ 60 %; exercise raises output to 20–25 L min⁻¹.
ECG: P = atrial depolarisation, QRS = ventricular depolarisation, T = ventricular repolarisation.
Arteries are thick-walled, valveless and high-pressure; veins are thin-walled, valved and low-pressure; the hepatic portal vein carries gut blood to the liver before the heart.

units.title: Excretory System
topics: Excretory organs and the structure of the nephron
Formation of urine and its regulation
Renal disorders

sections.title: Excretory organs and the structure of the nephron
Formation of urine and its regulation
Renal disorders

summary: The excretory organs are the kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra; the skin, lungs and liver are accessory routes, and the liver makes urea while the kidney excretes it.
Each kidney has about one million nephrons, in a cortex (corpuscles, convoluted tubules) and a medulla (pyramids, loops, collecting ducts) that drains through the pelvis into the ureter.
Ultrafiltration at the glomerulus passes water and small solutes but holds back cells and protein by pore size and negative charge; net pressure ≈ 10 mmHg, GFR ≈ 125 mL min⁻¹ (180 L day⁻¹).
Reabsorption recovers about 99 % of the filtrate: glucose and amino acids by active transport in the PCT (threshold 180 mg/dL, Tm 375 mg min⁻¹), water by osmosis.

The counter-current multiplier works because the descending limb is permeable to water and the ascending limb is not but pumps salt; the medulla is graded 300 → 1200 mOsm L⁻¹, and the vasa recta preserve the gradient.
Secretion adds H⁺, K⁺, NH₃, creatinine and drugs to the tubule and is the main route for acid removal.

ADH (made in the hypothalamus, stored in the posterior pituitary) concentrates urine; aldosterone retains Na⁺ and loses K⁺; ANP does the opposite. Diabetes insipidus = ADH problem = large dilute urine; diabetes mellitus = insulin problem = large glucose-containing urine.
Abnormal constituents: glucose (diabetes), protein (nephritis), ketones (starvation, ketoacidosis), blood (nephritis, stones), casts (tubular damage).

units.title: Nervous System and Sense Organs
topics: Central, peripheral and autonomic nervous systems
The nerve impulse and the synapse
The eye and the ear

sections.title: Central, peripheral and autonomic nervous systems
The nerve impulse and the synapse
The eye and the ear

summary: The CNS integrates information; the PNS connects it with receptors and effectors through cranial and spinal nerves.
Cerebral cortex supports conscious perception and voluntary action, while the hypothalamus, cerebellum and medulla have sharply testable special roles.
Spinal reflexes use dorsal sensory entry and ventral motor exit and can act before conscious perception.
Sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions differ in origin, fibre length, transmitter and typical visceral effects.
An action potential is an all-or-none, self-propagating reversal of membrane potential driven first by Na⁺ entry and then by K⁺ exit.
Myelination permits rapid saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier.
Chemical synapses use Ca²⁺-triggered transmitter release and are one-way, summable and pharmacologically vulnerable.
In the eye, the cornea supplies most fixed refraction, the lens accommodates, rods favour sensitivity and foveal cones favour acuity and colour.

units.title: Endocrine System
topics: Endocrine glands and their hormones
Hormonal disorders

sections.title: Endocrine glands and their hormones
Hormonal disorders

summary: Hormones are blood-borne messengers whose effects depend on receptors, chemical class, transport and feedback regulation.
The hypothalamus controls the anterior pituitary through portal blood and supplies the posterior pituitary with ADH and oxytocin.
Pituitary tropic hormones organise thyroid, adrenal-cortical and gonadal activity; GH and prolactin act more directly on non-endocrine tissues.
Thyroid hormones set metabolic rate and are essential to development; PTH and calcitonin act in opposite directions on blood calcium.
The adrenal cortex preserves salt, water and glucose during stress, whereas the medulla supplies a rapid catecholamine emergency response.
Insulin and glucagon form an antagonistic pair around blood glucose.
Endocrine diagnosis rests on direction and feedback: identify what is high, what is low and whether the controller is responding appropriately.
The major named disorders follow mechanically from hormone function, so symptoms can be derived rather than memorised in isolation.

units.title: Reproductive System
topics: Male and female reproductive organs
Gametogenesis
The ovarian and menstrual cycles

sections.title: Male and female reproductive organs
Gametogenesis
The ovarian and menstrual cycles

summary: The testes produce sperm in seminiferous tubules under FSH, testosterone and Sertoli-cell support; Leydig cells supply testosterone.
Sperm mature and are stored in the epididymis, then travel through the vas deferens and urethra in semen produced mainly by accessory glands.
The ovaries produce oocytes and steroid hormones; uterine tubes capture the oocyte and normally host fertilisation in the ampulla.
Spermatogenesis is continuous and quantitatively equal, whereas oogenesis begins before birth, is interrupted twice and conserves cytoplasm in one ovum.
Fertilisation restores diploidy, blocks polyspermy and initiates cleavage; the blastocyst implants in a progesterone-prepared endometrium.
The menstrual cycle is driven by changing feedback among GnRH, FSH/LH, oestrogen and progesterone.
Ovulation follows the LH surge, and the corpus luteum either regresses— causing menstruation—or is rescued by hCG in pregnancy.

units.title: Microbial Diseases and Immunology
topics: Typhoid, tuberculosis, HIV/AIDS, cholera, influenza, hepatitis and candidiasis
Innate and acquired immunity; antigens and antibodies
Vaccines: live attenuated, inactivated and toxoid

sections.title: Typhoid, tuberculosis, HIV/AIDS, cholera, influenza, hepatitis and candidiasis
Innate and acquired immunity; antigens and antibodies
Vaccines: live attenuated, inactivated and toxoid

summary: The named diseases separate cleanly by agent class, route and mechanism: water-borne typhoid/cholera, airborne TB/influenza, blood/sexual HIV and HBV/HCV, and opportunistic candidiasis.
TB's mycolic-acid wall explains acid-fast staining and macrophage survival; cholera toxin explains massive fluid loss without requiring bacteraemia.
HIV disables adaptive immunity at its CD4 coordinator and converts normal microbiota or ordinarily controlled organisms into opportunistic threats.
Influenza's segmented genome permits reassortment shifts as well as drift.
Hepatitis viruses A–E share a target organ but differ in genome, route, chronicity and vaccine strategy.
Innate defences act immediately and broadly; adaptive defences recognise epitopes specifically and remember them.
Antibody classes have distinct timing, location and effector roles, with IgM first and IgG dominant later.
Vaccines generate artificial active memory; their construction determines replication, strength, booster needs and cautions.

units.title: Medical Technology and Applied Biology
topics: Tissue and organ transplantation, in-vitro fertilization, amniocentesis and transgenic animals
Applied microbiology: dairy and beverage microbes, sewage and drinking-water treatment, bio-control agents

sections.title: Tissue and organ transplantation, IVF, amniocentesis and transgenic animals
Applied microbiology: dairy and beverage microbes, sewage and drinking-water treatment, bio-control agents

summary: Transplant compatibility is an immunological problem centred on HLA recognition; immunosuppression prevents rejection at the cost of infection risk.
IVF moves fertilisation to the laboratory, while ICSI additionally bypasses failures of sperm number, movement or oocyte penetration.
Amniocentesis provides fetal cells for definitive chromosome/DNA diagnosis, but as an invasive test it follows careful counselling and screening.
Transgenic animals produce disease models and valuable proteins, yet require welfare, containment and biosafety oversight.
Dairy and beverage industries are controlled fermentations whose acids, gases and ethanol explain product texture, preservation and flavour.
Sewage treatment relocates microbial oxidation from rivers to engineered aeration systems and extracts energy from sludge by anaerobic digestion.
Drinking-water safety is a multi-barrier process monitored with faecal indicator organisms.
Biocontrol uses ecological specificity—especially Bt, baculoviruses and Trichoderma—as an alternative or complement to chemical pesticides.

sections.title: Animal behaviour: reflex actions, taxes and migration
Air, water and soil pollution; pesticides
Aquatic, terrestrial and volant adaptations
Conservation biology: biodiversity, protected areas, hotspots, Ramsar sites, IUCN categories and endangered species of Nepal

summary: Reflexes, taxes and kineses differ by pathway, body involvement and whether movement is directed.
Migration trades travel costs for seasonal access to food and breeding habitat and relies on multiple navigational cues.
Air pollution separates into particles/toxic gases, smog, acid deposition, ozone depletion and greenhouse warming.
Water and soil pollutants may be biodegradable, nutrient-like or persistent; persistence plus fat solubility creates biomagnification.
Aquatic and terrestrial animals solve opposite mechanical/osmotic problems, while flight imposes the strictest combined demands for lift, power and low mass.
Biodiversity includes genes, species and ecosystems, and evenness matters as well as species count.
In-situ protected areas preserve whole systems; ex-situ collections are a complementary safety net.
Hotspots and Ramsar sites prioritise exceptional endemic-rich and wetland ecosystems under threat.
